## F1-P
1) 17:20–17:28, ticket room: Neri feels the single token in her right coat pocket while Olin presses for it. She asks for one reason without begging; he answers only that someone on the far bank needs him. Setup: token weight and clock. At 17:28 her consequential choice is to press the token into his palm: “One trip. One.” 2) 17:28–17:40, landing: the eight-minute walk leaves no room to recover it honestly. Olin’s agency: he accepts the token, keeps the destination unnamed, and heads for the ferry, forcing Neri to walk beside a decision already made. 3) 17:40–17:52, crossing: the token admits exactly one and is consumed; Olin boards alone while Neri stays on the near bank. 4) 17:52–17:55, gate: the apprenticeship gate closes before any exception; Neri accepts the fixed limit—one token, one passenger, no rescue—and touches her empty right pocket. Payoff: the pocket that held the token at 17:20 is empty at 17:55. Author-side motive may be planned, but Neri and the reader do not know it at 17:20.

## F1-D
The ticket-room clock said 17:20 when Olin leaned across the counter, close enough that Neri could smell the river on his coat. The room smelled of ink and cold metal. The token sat in her right coat pocket, small and companioned, the only thing in the room that could not be argued with. She kept her thumb hooked through the pocket lining.

“Give it to me,” Olin said.

“Say why,” Neri said. “Not a speech. A name.”

He looked at the ferry schedule as if it might confess for him. “Someone on the far bank needs me tonight.”

“That is a weather report, not a reason.”

The clock moved one minute. Neri could hear the ticket machine breathe. She thought of the apprenticeship gate at 17:55, of twelve minutes on the water, of the eight-minute walk already spent in her legs. She thought of the way Olin used to save her a seat, before they learned to use each other instead. She had not planned to make a gift of it; she had planned only to make him say something true.

“Last ferry,” she said. “It does not wait, and neither do I.”

Olin’s hand opened on the counter, palm up, patient as a locked door. “One trip. One.”

Neri looked at his palm, then at her right pocket. The token was warm from her body; the counter was cold. She pulled it out, felt its edge bite her fingertip, and set it in his hand. She closed his fingers over it herself, so custody would not be a later argument.

“There,” she said. “One trip. One. You still owe me a name.”

Olin turned toward the door without answering. The clock said 17:28. Neri stood with her empty right hand in her pocket, listening to the token change pockets.

State delta: 17:28 — token transferred from Neri’s right coat pocket to Olin’s closed hand; Neri has no token and cannot cross tonight; Olin’s motive remains unnamed; the 17:55 gate is unreachable for Neri.

## F2-P
1) 12:00–12:05, booth doorway: Rafi starts with the key on the desk and wants Leena to ask for him, not just the room. She asks for quiet for Pia’s violin take; Pia watches the clock. Setup: the key on the desk and the 12:20 hard stop. 2) 12:05, commitment: Rafi’s consequential choice is to hand the key to Leena and point to Pia: “Fifteen minutes. Pia first.” The remaining slot is committed to one recording; his audition cannot be made. Leena’s agency: she does not ask for Rafi or name the bargain; she takes the key and shields Pia from the argument. Pia’s agency: she tunes unprompted, making the choice concrete. 3) 12:05–12:20, recording: Pia records one uninterrupted take; Rafi stays outside with the returned key, knowing a joint take or fragments would satisfy no one. 4) 12:20–12:30, aftermath: the next group enters; Rafi has no audition take and accepts the fixed limit—one booth, one complete fifteen-minute take, no extension. Earned outcome: he keeps the loss practical, not healed: “Just the room. Not forgiveness.” Payoff: the key starts on the desk and ends in Rafi’s pocket, handed over and returned. Author-side only: Leena’s reason for leaving the band may be planned, but Rafi and the reader do not know it at 12:00.

## F2-D
The booth key lay on the desk like a dare at 12:00. Rafi put his hand over it before Leena reached the doorway, then took his hand away, because hiding it would be a speech.

“Pia needs quiet,” Leena said. “Fifteen minutes. You’ve got until 12:20.”

“I’ve got a take,” Rafi said. “Also fifteen. Also due at 12:30.”

Pia stood beside her mother with the violin case bumping her knee. She looked at the booth, then at Rafi, then at the floor, as if the schedule might be a shy animal.

Rafi was tired of being useful only when something was needed. He had been the reliable one long enough to know the invoice always arrived later.

Leena’s shoulder lifted. “We could have half an hour,” she said, as if wanting it might extend the booking.

“Twenty,” Rafi said. “The next group has the room, and the room has rules.”

He moved the key from the desk to his palm. The metal was warm from the desk. Pia’s eyes followed it like a coin. Leena did not ask for Rafi; she asked for the door, and Rafi heard the difference.

“It ain’t a favor,” Leena said, “if you keep an account.”

Rafi looked at Pia, who had already unlatched her case and was sawing a single open string, testing the room. He put the key in Leena’s hand and closed her fingers around it.

“Fifteen minutes,” he said. “Pia first. My audition can be late.”

Leena’s mouth tightened, not smiling. “Just the room. Not forgiveness.”

“I know,” Rafi said.

The clock reached 12:05. The key was in Leena’s hand; the booth was committed to one violin take, and Rafi’s fifteen minutes were already spent.

State delta: 12:05 — booth key moved from desk to Leena’s closed hand; remaining slot committed to Pia’s 12:05–12:20 take; Rafi has no audition recording and accepts the 12:20 hard stop.
